title: Isomerism
summary: Isomerism describes compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms. This lesson explains structural, geometric (cis/trans), and optical isomerism with clear examples.
objectives: Identify structural, geometric, and optical isomers from molecular formulas and drawings
Draw cis and trans isomers of simple alkenes
Explain how chiral centers create optical isomers
Predict which isomers are optically active
prerequisites: Students should already know basic carbon bonding, how to draw Lewis structures, and the meaning of functional groups.
why: Isomers give the same atoms different properties, which is why drugs, plastics, and fuels can behave very differently even though they share a formula. Understanding isomerism helps chemists design safer medicines and more efficient materials.

In everyday life, the taste of sugar versus its mirror‑image counterpart, or the smell of limonene in oranges versus lemons, is due to isomerism. Recognising these differences is essential for fields like pharmacology, food science, and environmental chemistry.

sections.heading: What Is Isomerism?
sections.body:
Imagine you have a set of LEGO bricks that all together weigh the same amount. Even though the total weight is identical, you can snap the bricks together in many different ways – a tall tower, a wide base, or a winding staircase. In chemistry, the “bricks” are atoms, and the “total weight” is the molecular formula (the number and type of atoms). **Isomerism** is the phenomenon where compounds share the same molecular formula but are assembled differently, giving them distinct shapes and properties.

> **Definition:** *Isomerism* is the existence of two or more compounds that have exactly the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms in space.

Why does this happen? Atoms can bond in several patterns because chemical bonds are flexible. A carbon atom, for example, can form four single bonds, two double bonds, or a triple bond, and these possibilities lead to many ways of connecting the same set of atoms. When the connections differ, the resulting molecules behave differently – they may smell different, melt at different temperatures, or react in unique ways.

Chemists group isomers into three main families:

1. **Structural (or constitutional) isomers** – the atoms are linked in a different order. Think of rearranging the rooms in a house: the same walls and floor area are present, but the kitchen might be where the bedroom was, changing how you use the space.

2. **Geometric (cis/trans) isomers** – the atoms are connected in the same order, but they occupy different positions around a rigid double bond or a ring. Picture a book that can be opened either “face‑up” (cis) or “face‑down” (trans); the pages are the same, but the orientation changes how the book sits on a shelf.

3. **Optical (chiral) isomers** – the molecule and its mirror image cannot be superimposed, much like left and right hands. If you try to place your left hand on top of your right hand, the thumbs point in opposite directions; no amount of turning will make them match. Such molecules rotate plane‑polarized light, a property called optical activity.

> **Note:** The three types are not mutually exclusive. A single compound can have both structural and geometric isomerism, or geometric and optical isomerism, depending on its size and the presence of double bonds or chiral centers.

To see how the same formula can give different structures, consider the simple formula $C_4H_{10}$. One arrangement is **butane**, a straight chain of four carbon atoms:

$$\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$$

Another arrangement is **isobutane**, where three carbons form a branch off a central carbon:

$$\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{C}$$

Both contain four carbon and ten hydrogen atoms, yet their shapes differ enough that butane boils at $-0.5^\circ\text{C}$ while isobutane boils at $-11.7^\circ\text{C}$. The difference matters in everyday life – gasoline engines rely on specific isomers to run efficiently.

> **In daily life:** The sweet smell of menthol and the bitter taste of camphor come from molecules that have the same atoms but are arranged differently; they are structural isomers of each other.

Understanding isomerism is useful because it helps chemists predict how a molecule will behave, design drugs that fit precisely into biological targets, and create materials with desired physical properties. When you hear that “the same formula can give different results,” remember that the hidden variable is *how* the atoms are put together.

> **Remember:** If two compounds have the same molecular formula, always ask – are the atoms connected differently (structural), positioned differently around a rigid bond (geometric), or arranged as non‑superimposable mirror images (optical)? This question guides you to the correct type of isomerism.

sections.heading: Structural (Constitutional) Isomers
sections.body:
When we talk about **structural (or constitutional) isomers**, we mean molecules that have exactly the same numbers of each type of atom – the same molecular formula – but those atoms are linked together in a different order.  
The way the atoms are *connected* (the “bonding pattern”) changes the shape of the molecule, and that often changes its physical properties such as boiling point, density, or how it smells.

> **Definition:** Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different connectivity of atoms.

---

### Why does connectivity matter?

Think of a set of LEGO bricks. You have four red bricks and ten blue bricks. You can snap them together to make a straight line, or you can branch one brick out to the side. Both constructions use the same bricks, but they look different and you can build different things with them. In chemistry, the “bricks” are atoms, and the “snaps” are chemical bonds. Changing the pattern of snaps gives a new molecule, even though the count of each brick stays the same.

---

### Simple example: C₄H₁₀ – butane vs. isobutane  

The formula C₄H₁₀ tells us there are four carbon atoms and ten hydrogen atoms. There are two common ways to join those carbons:

1. **Normal (n‑)butane** – a straight chain of four carbons.  
   ```
   CH3–CH2–CH2–CH3
   ```
   Each carbon in the middle is bonded to two other carbons; the ends are bonded to only one carbon.

2. **Isobutane** (also called methylpropane) – a three‑carbon chain with a side branch.  
   ```
        CH3
        |
   CH3–C–CH3
   ```
   Here three carbons form a line, and the fourth carbon is attached as a side group (a “branch”).

Both drawings contain the same atoms, but the **connectivity** is different, so they are structural isomers.

> **In daily life:** n‑butane is a component of gasoline, while isobutane is used as a refrigerant and in aerosol propellants. Their different structures give them different boiling points, which makes each useful for a specific purpose.

---

### How to recognise a new structural isomer

When you are given a molecular formula, ask yourself:

1. **How many carbon skeletons can you make?**  
   Start with the longest possible chain, then try shortening it and adding branches.

2. **Can any functional groups be placed in different positions?**  
   For example, C₃H₆O could be an aldehyde (propanal) or a ketone (acetone). The carbonyl group is the same atom (C=O) but its location changes the connectivity.

3. **Are there any rings possible?**  
   With enough carbons, you can close a chain into a ring. Cyclobutane (a four‑membered ring) also has the formula C₄H₈, which is a different type of isomer from the open‑chain alkenes.

---

### Simple drawing exercise

1. **Write the formula C₅H₁₂.**  
2. **Draw the straight‑chain version** (pentane):  
   ```
   CH3–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH3
   ```
3. **Create a branch** by moving one CH₃ group onto the second carbon:  
   ```
        CH3
        |
   CH3–CH–CH2–CH3
   ```
4. **Make a different branch** by attaching the CH₃ to the middle carbon:  
   ```
        CH3
        |
   CH3–CH–CH3
        |
       CH3
   ```
   (This is 2‑methylbutane.)  

Count the carbons and hydrogens each time to verify you still have C₅H₁₂. Each drawing is a distinct structural isomer.

---

### Why you should care

Even a tiny change in connectivity can alter how a molecule interacts with other substances. In medicines, one structural isomer may be an effective drug while another is inactive or even harmful. In fuels, different isomers burn at slightly different rates, affecting engine performance.

> **Remember:** Two compounds with the same formula are not automatically the same substance – check how the atoms are linked.

By practising the “draw‑and‑count” method, you will quickly learn to spot all possible structural isomers for a given formula. This skill is the foundation for later topics such as stereochemistry and reaction mechanisms.

sections.heading: Geometric (Cis/Trans) Isomerism
sections.body:
When two atoms are joined by a double bond, the bond acts like a short, stiff bridge.  
Unlike a single bond, which can rotate freely like a swivel chair, a double bond is locked in place – the two carbon atoms cannot turn around each other. This “restricted rotation” means that the groups attached to each carbon stay on the same side of the bridge, and the relative positions become important.

> **Definition:** *Geometric (cis/trans) isomerism* occurs when compounds have the same atoms connected in the same order, but the atoms are arranged differently in space because rotation around a double bond is blocked.

Imagine a road with a median strip. Cars on the left side must stay on the left, and cars on the right must stay on the right; they cannot cross the median without a bridge. In a molecule with a double bond, the “median” is the double bond itself, and the “cars” are the groups attached to the carbons. Because they cannot cross, two distinct arrangements are possible.

### Cis and trans labels

- **Cis** (Latin for “on this side”) – the two substituent groups of interest are on the same side of the double bond.
- **Trans** (Latin for “across”) – the two groups are on opposite sides of the double bond.

These labels are most useful when each carbon of the double bond carries one identical substituent (often a hydrogen) and one different substituent. The identical substituents help us decide which side to compare.

#### Example 1: 2‑butene

The formula for 2‑butene is $C_4H_8$. Its skeleton is  

$$\text{CH}_3\!-\!CH\!=\!CH\!-\!\text{CH}_3$$  

Each double‑bonded carbon is attached to a methyl group ($\text{CH}_3$) and a hydrogen ($\text{H}$).  

- **Cis‑2‑butene**: the two methyl groups are on the same side of the double bond.  
  Sketch:  

  ```
  H   CH3
   \ /
    C=C
   / \
 CH3   H
  ```

- **Trans‑2‑butene**: the methyl groups are on opposite sides.  

  ```
  CH3   H
   \   /
    C=C
   /   \
  H    CH3
  ```

Because the groups are arranged differently, the molecules have different shapes. The cis form is bent, giving a larger surface area that can attract other molecules more strongly. The trans form is more linear, allowing the molecules to pack together more tightly.

#### Example 2: 1,2‑dichloroethene

The formula is $C_2H_2Cl_2$, written as  

$$\text{Cl}\!-\!CH\!=\!CH\!-\!\text{Cl}$$  

Each carbon of the double bond carries one chlorine ($\text{Cl}$) and one hydrogen ($\text{H}$).

- **Cis‑1,2‑dichloroethene**: the two chlorine atoms sit on the same side.  
- **Trans‑1,2‑dichloroethene**: the chlorine atoms are opposite each other.

### Physical property differences

Even though the two isomers have exactly the same atoms, their boiling points, melting points, and densities can differ noticeably.

| Isomer | Boiling point (°C) | Melting point (°C) |
|--------|-------------------|--------------------|
| cis‑2‑butene | 3.7 | –138 |
| trans‑2‑butene | 0.9 | –184 |
| cis‑1,2‑dichloroethene | 60 | –44 |
| trans‑1,2‑dichloroethene | 47 | –101 |

Why the difference? In the **cis** isomers, the like groups (e.g., the two methyl groups in cis‑2‑butene) are closer together, creating a larger dipole moment. This stronger dipole leads to stronger intermolecular attractions, raising the boiling point. The **trans** isomers are more symmetrical; their dipoles cancel, so they interact less strongly and boil at lower temperatures.

> **Note:** The terms *cis* and *trans* are only reliable when each carbon of the double bond has one identical substituent. If both substituents are different on each carbon, the more general *E/Z* system must be used.

### Why it matters

Geometric isomerism influences how a molecule behaves in the real world. For example, the cis form of a fatty acid can make cell membranes more fluid, while the trans form makes them rigid. In pharmaceuticals, one isomer may be therapeutic while the other is inactive or even harmful. Recognizing cis/trans patterns helps chemists predict these effects and design better drugs, materials, and foods.

> **In daily life:** The difference between cis‑ and trans‑fatty acids in cooking oil is a direct result of geometric isomerism. Trans fats (the *trans* isomers) are created during industrial hydrogenation and have been linked to heart disease, whereas natural cis fats are generally healthier.

Understanding geometric isomerism is therefore a practical tool: it lets us read a simple drawing and immediately anticipate how a molecule might smell, melt, or interact with the body.

sections.heading: Chirality and Optical Isomerism
sections.body:
When we talk about **chirality** we are really talking about “handedness”.  
Imagine your left and right hands. They look the same at a glance, but if you try to place one on top of the other they will never line up perfectly – they are *non‑superimposable* mirror images. Molecules can behave the same way.

> **Definition:** *A chiral molecule is one that cannot be rotated or flipped so that it exactly matches its own mirror image.*

The most common source of molecular chirality is a **chiral centre** (also called an *asymmetric carbon*). This is a carbon atom that is attached to four different groups. Because the four substituents are all distinct, the carbon becomes a three‑dimensional “pivot” that can point in two different directions, giving two mirror‑image forms called **enantiomers**.

Why does a carbon need four different groups? Carbon normally forms four single bonds. If any two of those bonds are to the same group, you can rotate the molecule and make the two sides look the same – the molecule would be *superimposable* on its mirror image and therefore achiral. Only when each of the four bonds leads to a unique group does the carbon become a true “handed” centre.

### Lactic acid – a simple example

Lactic acid has the formula $$\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)COOH}$$.  
Look at the central carbon (the one marked with the parentheses). It is attached to:

1. a methyl group ($\mathrm{CH_3}$)  
2. a hydroxyl group ($\mathrm{OH}$)  
3. a carboxyl group ($\mathrm{COOH}$)  
4. a hydrogen atom ($\mathrm{H}$)

All four are different, so this carbon is a chiral centre. If we draw the molecule on paper and then draw its mirror image, we obtain two structures that cannot be placed on top of each other no matter how we turn them. Chemists label these two forms **(R)-lactic acid** and **(S)-lactic acid** (R and S stand for *rectus* and *sinister*, Latin for right and left).

> **In daily life:** The two forms of lactic acid taste slightly different and are processed differently by our bodies. In many foods, only one enantiomer is naturally present, which is why the flavor is consistent.

### How do we know which is which?

To assign the R or S label we use the **Cahn‑Ingold‑Prelog (CIP) priority rules**:

1. Rank the four substituents attached to the chiral carbon by atomic number (higher = higher priority).  
2. Orient the molecule so the lowest‑priority group (usually hydrogen) points away from you.  
3. Look at the sequence 1 → 2 → 3. If the arrow goes clockwise, the configuration is **R**; if counter‑clockwise, it is **S**.

Applying the rules to lactic acid:

- $\mathrm{COOH}$ (carbon attached to two oxygens) gets priority 1.  
- $\mathrm{OH}$ (oxygen) gets priority 2.  
- $\mathrm{CH_3}$ (carbon attached only to hydrogens) gets priority 3.  
- $\mathrm{H}$ gets priority 4 (lowest).

When the molecule is drawn with the hydrogen pointing back, the 1‑2‑3 sequence is clockwise, so the common natural form is **(S)-lactic acid**.

> **Note:** The terms *right‑handed* and *left‑handed* do **not** always correspond to R and S. Always use the CIP rules; guessing can lead to the **Common mistake:** mixing up the two labels.

### Why does chirality matter?

Enantiomers often have dramatically different biological effects. One might be a useful drug, while its mirror image could be inactive or even harmful. A famous case is thalidomide: one enantiomer eased morning sickness, the other caused severe birth defects. Understanding chirality lets chemists design safer medicines, create better flavors, and develop materials with special optical properties.

In summary, a chiral centre is a carbon bonded to four different groups, creating two non‑superimposable mirror images. Lactic acid illustrates the idea clearly: its central carbon meets the definition, leading to (R)- and (S)-forms that behave differently in nature and industry. Recognizing and naming these forms is a fundamental skill in organic chemistry.

sections.heading: Detecting Optical Activity
sections.body:
When a beam of white light passes through a clear liquid, most people think nothing will happen – the light just keeps going straight.  
If the liquid contains **chiral** molecules (molecules that are not superimposable on their mirror image), the light does something surprising: its plane of vibration rotates. This phenomenon is called **optical activity**.

> **Definition:** *Optical activity* is the ability of a chiral substance to rotate the plane of polarized light as the light travels through it.

### Why does the rotation happen?

Light can be thought of as an electromagnetic wave that vibrates in many directions. If we place a special filter called a **polarizer** in the path of the light, only vibrations in one direction are allowed to pass. The resulting light is **plane‑polarized** – all its electric fields swing in the same plane.

When this plane‑polarized light meets a chiral molecule, the molecule’s asymmetric shape interacts slightly differently with the electric field depending on the direction of the field. The interaction is not strong enough to stop the light, but it nudges the vibration plane a little, turning it clockwise or counter‑clockwise. The direction of turn depends on the molecule’s handedness:

* The **(R)-** or **(+)-** enantiomer rotates light to the right (clockwise).  
* The **(S)-** or **(–)-** enantiomer rotates light to the left (counter‑clockwise).

Think of a screw: a right‑handed screw moves forward when you turn it clockwise, while a left‑handed screw moves forward when you turn it counter‑clockwise. The molecule’s “handedness” tells the light which way to turn, just as the screw’s thread tells you which direction to turn to advance.

> **Note:** The amount of rotation depends on three factors: the concentration of the chiral substance, the length of the light path through the sample, and the wavelength (color) of the light. This relationship is expressed by the equation $$\alpha = [\alpha]_{\text{D}} \, c \, l$$ where $\alpha$ is the observed rotation, $[\alpha]_{\text{D}}$ is the **specific rotation** (a constant for each pure enantiomer at a given temperature and wavelength), $c$ is concentration (in g · mL⁻¹), and $l$ is path length (in dm).

### How do we measure the rotation?

A **polarimeter** is a simple instrument that does exactly this. It has three main parts:

1. **Light source** – usually a sodium lamp that emits a single wavelength (the D‑line at 589 nm).  
2. **Polarizer** – creates plane‑polarized light.  
3. **Analyzer** – another polarizer that can be rotated until the light intensity reaching a detector is minimized (the dark point).  

When the sample tube is placed between the polarizer and analyzer, the analyzer must be turned a little farther (or less) than the original dark position to regain darkness. The angle through which the analyzer is turned is the observed rotation $\alpha$.

> **In daily life:** Polarimeters are used to check the purity of sugars, pharmaceuticals, and essential oils. If a sample should be pure (+)-lactic acid but the measured rotation is smaller than expected, it tells the chemist that some (–)-lactic acid is present as an impurity.

### Thought experiment – a mini‑lab

Imagine you have two identical glass tubes, each 10 cm long. Fill one with a solution of pure (+)-limonene (the smell of oranges) and the other with pure (–)-limonene (the smell of pine). Place both tubes in a polarimeter one after the other, using the same concentration.

1. **Observe**: The analyzer must be turned 15° clockwise for the (+) tube to reach darkness, and 15° counter‑clockwise for the (–) tube.  
2. **Interpret**: The equal magnitude tells you the two solutions have the same concentration and path length; the opposite signs confirm they are opposite enantiomers.  
3. **Mix**: Now pour equal volumes of the two solutions together in a third tube. Measure again – the analyzer now needs almost no rotation because the opposite rotations cancel. This demonstrates that a racemic (50/50) mixture is **optically inactive**, even though each molecule is still chiral.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that any mixture of chiral compounds will rotate light. Only a mixture with an excess of one enantiomer shows net rotation; a perfect 1:1 mixture gives zero rotation.

By understanding how a polarimeter works and why enantiomers rotate light in opposite directions, you gain a powerful, non‑destructive tool for identifying and quantifying chirality in the laboratory and industry.

sections.heading: Comparing the Three Types
sections.body:
> **Definition:** Isomers are compounds that have the same molecular formula (same number and type of atoms) but differ in how those atoms are arranged or oriented.  

When we compare the three main families—**structural (constitutional) isomers**, **geometric (cis/trans) isomers**, and **optical (chiral) isomers**—we look at three aspects: the type of bonding changes, the shape of the molecule, and the physical properties that we can measure.

### 1. What changes in the bonds?  

* **Structural isomers** break and remake single bonds. The atoms are connected in a different order, so the *connectivity* (which atom is attached to which) is different.  
* **Geometric isomers** keep the same connectivity; the same atoms are linked to the same neighbors, but a double bond or a ring prevents free rotation. The *relative positions* of groups around that restricted bond change.  
* **Optical isomers** also keep the same connectivity and the same arrangement around double bonds, but they contain a *chiral centre*—a carbon attached to four different groups. This creates two non‑superimposable mirror images, like left and right hands.

### 2. How does the shape differ?  

* In **structural isomers**, the overall shape can be very different because the skeleton of the molecule is rearranged. For example, butane (CH₃‑CH₂‑CH₂‑CH₃) and isobutane (CH₃‑CH(CH₃)‑CH₃) have the same formula C₄H₁₀ but one is a straight chain and the other is branched.  
* In **geometric isomers**, the shape changes only around the restricted bond. The classic example is 2‑butene: the *cis* form has the two methyl groups on the same side, while the *trans* form has them on opposite sides. The rest of the molecule stays the same.  
* In **optical isomers**, the shape is the same except that the molecule is a mirror image of itself. Imagine a screw‑driver: a right‑handed and a left‑handed screwdriver look identical from a distance, but they fit opposite threads.

### 3. Physical properties you can measure  

| Property | Structural Isomers | Geometric Isomers | Optical Isomers |
|----------|-------------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| **Boiling point** | Often different because surface area changes (branched = lower boiling). | Usually close, but *cis* may have higher boiling due to dipole‑dipole attraction. | Identical for a pair (enantiomers) unless in a chiral environment. |
| **Melting point** | Can vary widely. | May differ; *cis* often lower melting because crystals are less tightly packed. | Identical for a pure pair; racemic mixtures may have higher melting points. |
| **Density** | May differ if shape changes volume. | Very similar; only orientation changes. | Same for each enantiomer. |
| **Optical activity** | No rotation of plane‑polarized light. | No rotation. | Rotates plane‑polarized light: one enantiomer rotates clockwise (d‑ or (+)), the other counter‑clockwise (l‑ or (‑)). |
| **Reactivity** | Can differ dramatically (e.g., alcohol vs. ether). | May differ in reactions that depend on steric hindrance. | Often identical in achiral reagents; different in chiral catalysts or enzymes. |

> **Note:** Even though optical isomers have the same melting point, a *racemic mixture* (equal amounts of both) can crystallize in a way that gives a higher melting point than either pure enantiomer.  

### 4. Why does the comparison matter?  

Understanding the differences helps chemists predict how a molecule will behave in real life. For instance, the drug **ibuprofen** exists as two enantiomers; only one is active as a pain reliever, while the other is less effective. Knowing that it is an *optical* isomer tells us we must separate the two mirror images.  

In contrast, **butane** and **isobutane** are structural isomers with very different boiling points, so they are used for different fuel applications.  

Geometric isomers like **cis‑hex-2‑ene** and **trans‑hex-2‑ene** have different smells because the arrangement of groups changes how they interact with odor receptors.

> **In daily life:** Think of structural isomers as different LEGO constructions using the same bricks, geometric isomers as the same LEGO piece turned upside‑down, and optical isomers as left‑handed and right‑handed gloves—same material, opposite handedness.

> **Common mistake:** Students often think “same formula = same properties.” The table shows that even tiny changes in arrangement can lead to big differences in boiling point, smell, or biological activity.

By keeping track of **bond connectivity**, **spatial arrangement**, and **measurable properties**, you can quickly decide which type of isomer you are dealing with and why it matters in the laboratory or in everyday products.

sections.heading: Practice Problems and Real‑World Applications
sections.body:
> **Definition:** *Isomer* – molecules that have the same molecular formula (same numbers of each type of atom) but different arrangements of those atoms.

When you finish learning about the three kinds of isomerism, the best way to remember them is to **practice**. Below are short exercises that let you identify the type of isomer, draw the correct structures, label chiral centers, and decide whether a compound will rotate plane‑polarized light. After the problems, you will see how these ideas appear in everyday products such as medicines and fragrances.

---

### 1. Identify the isomer type  

**Exercise 1** – Look at the two formulas below. Both have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O.

| A | B |
|---|---|
| CH₃‑CH₂‑CH₂‑CH₂‑OH | CH₃‑CH(OH)‑CH₃‑CH₃ |

*Question:* Which pair of compounds are **structural (constitutional) isomers**? Explain in one sentence.

*Hint:* Structural isomers differ in the **connectivity** – which atoms are directly bonded to each other.

---

### 2. Draw a cis/trans pair  

**Exercise 2** – Draw the two possible geometric isomers of 2‑butene, a four‑carbon alkene with a double bond between C₂ and C₃.

*Steps:*  

1. Write the carbon skeleton: CH₃‑CH=CH‑CH₃.  
2. Add the substituents on each carbon of the double bond.  
3. For the **cis** isomer, place the two CH₃ groups on the same side of the double bond.  
4. For the **trans** isomer, place them on opposite sides.

*Why it matters:* The double bond cannot rotate, so the two arrangements are locked in place and have different physical properties (e.g., boiling point).

---

### 3. Label chiral centers  

**Exercise 3** – Consider the molecule 2‑bromobutane: CH₃‑CH(Br)‑CH₂‑CH₃.

*Task:*  

1. Identify the carbon atom that is attached to four different groups.  
2. Circle that carbon and label it as a **chiral center**.  
3. Write the two possible configurations (R and S) using the Cahn‑Ingold‑Prelog priority rules (you do not need to draw the full 3‑D wedge‑dash picture, just state which group gets highest priority).

*Explanation:* A **chiral center** is a carbon with four distinct substituents, leading to non‑superimposable mirror images called **enantiomers**.

---

### 4. Predict optical activity  

**Exercise 4** – A solution contains only one of the enantiomers of (R)-lactic acid.  

*Question:* Will this solution rotate plane‑polarized light? If yes, in which direction (clockwise = dextrorotatory, counter‑clockwise = levorotatory)?

*Answer format:* “Yes, it is **[d‑/l‑]** because …”  

*Note:* Optical activity occurs only when a molecule is **chiral** and exists as a single enantiomer, not as a racemic (50/50) mixture.

---

### 5. Real‑world connections  

**Pharmaceuticals** – Many drugs are chiral. For example, the painkiller **ibuprofen** is sold as a racemic mixture, but only the (S)-enantiomer is active. The (R)-form is essentially a waste product that the body must convert. This explains why the **dose** and **side‑effects** can differ between the two forms.

**Fragrances** – The scent of **carvone** differs dramatically between its two enantiomers: (R)-carvone smells like spearmint, while (S)-carvone smells like caraway seeds. The same molecular formula, but different **spatial arrangement** gives completely different olfactory experiences.

**Food additives** – The sweetener **aspartame** contains two chiral centers. Only one specific combination of configurations (L‑α‑aspartyl‑L‑phenylalanine methyl ester) provides the sweet taste; the other stereoisomers are either bitter or tasteless.

> **In daily life:** When you buy a medication, a perfume, or even a chewing‑gum, you are often getting a specific isomer that has been chosen for its desired effect.

---

### Quick check  

| Problem | Answer (short) |
|---------|----------------|
| 1 – Isomer type | Structural isomers (different connectivity). |
| 2 – Cis/trans | Cis: CH₃ groups same side; Trans: opposite sides. |
| 3 – Chiral center | Carbon‑2 is chiral; configurations R/S depend on priority (Br > CH₃ > CH₂CH₃ > H). |
| 4 – Optical activity | Yes, it is dextrorotatory (d‑) because the (R)-enantiomer of lactic acid rotates light clockwise. |

Working through these exercises will help you see how the abstract idea of “same formula, different shape” translates into real products that affect health, flavor, and fragrance. Keep practicing by drawing your own examples, and you’ll soon spot isomerism everywhere!

examples.title: Identify a constitutional isomer
examples.given: Draw the structural formula for C₄H₁₀ and decide if two given drawings are the same compound or isomers.

steps.label: Write formula
steps.text: Write C₄H₁₀ to know how many C and H atoms must appear.

steps.label: Count bonds
steps.text: Verify each carbon makes four bonds; each hydrogen makes one.

steps.label: Compare connectivity
steps.text: Look at how the carbon atoms are linked in each drawing.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: If the carbon skeletons differ, the drawings are constitutional isomers.

examples.answer: The two drawings with a straight chain and a branched chain are constitutional isomers of C₄H₁₀.

examples.title: Determine cis/trans geometry
examples.given: A molecule with formula C₂H₂Cl₂ has the double bond CHCl=CHCl. Decide whether the given drawing is the cis or trans isomer.

steps.label: Identify substituents
steps.text: Locate the two chlorine atoms attached to the double‑bonded carbons.

steps.label: Check relative position
steps.text: See if the Cl atoms are on the same side of the double bond.

steps.label: Apply cis/trans rule
steps.text: Same side → cis; opposite sides → trans.

steps.label: State isomerism
steps.text: Record the geometry based on the observation.

examples.answer: The Cl atoms are on opposite sides of the double bond, so the molecule is the trans isomer of C₂H₂Cl₂.

examples.title: Classify optical activity and assign R/S configuration
examples.given: The compound (2‑bromo‑3‑chlorobutane) has the stereocenter at carbon‑2. Determine if it is optically active and assign its absolute configuration.

steps.label: Identify chiral center
steps.text: Carbon‑2 is attached to four different groups (Br, CH₃, CH₂Cl, H).

steps.label: Assign priorities
steps.text: Rank substituents by atomic number: Br (1) > Cl (2) > CH₃ (3) > H (4).

steps.label: Orient molecule
steps.text: Rotate the molecule so the lowest priority (H) points away from you.

steps.label: Determine order
steps.text: Observe the sequence 1 → 2 → 3; if clockwise → R, counter‑clockwise → S.

steps.label: Conclude optical activity
steps.text: A single chiral center gives one enantiomer, so the compound is optically active.

examples.answer: With the given orientation the 1‑2‑3 sequence is clockwise, giving the R configuration; the molecule is optically active as the (R)-2‑bromo‑3‑chlorobutane enantiomer.

practice.q: Draw the structural formulas of two constitutional isomers of C₃H₆O.
practice.a:
Step 1: Identify possible functional groups. With C₃H₆O we can have an aldehyde, ketone, or an alcohol + alkene.
Step 2: Aldehyde isomer – propanal: CH₃‑CH₂‑CHO.
Step 3: Ketone isomer – acetone: CH₃‑CO‑CH₃.
Both have the same molecular formula C₃H₆O but different connectivity, so they are constitutional isomers.

practice.q: A compound has the formula C₂H₄Cl₂ and exists as a cis‑trans pair. Draw both geometric isomers.
practice.a:
Step 1: Two chlorine atoms must be attached to the two carbon atoms of a C=C double bond.
Step 2: Cis isomer – both Cl atoms on the same side of the double bond:
Cl‑CH=CH‑Cl (with both Cl on the same side).
Step 3: Trans isomer – the Cl atoms on opposite sides of the double bond:
Cl‑CH=CH‑Cl (with Cl on opposite sides).
These two drawings represent the cis and trans geometric isomers.

practice.q: Determine whether 2‑butanol (CH₃‑CH(OH)‑CH₂‑CH₃) is chiral. If it is, draw its enantiomers and indicate the direction of optical rotation qualitatively.
practice.a:
Step 1: Identify the carbon bearing the OH group – carbon‑2.
Step 2: Check its four substituents: –CH₃, –CH₂CH₃, –OH, and –H. All are different, so carbon‑2 is a stereocenter → the molecule is chiral.
Step 3: Draw the two possible configurations (R and S). Using the Cahn‑Ingold‑Prelog rules, assign priorities: OH (1) > CH₂CH₃ (2) > CH₃ (3) > H (4).
Step 4: Arrange the groups so that the lowest priority (H) is behind the plane.
- If the sequence 1→2→3 is clockwise, the configuration is R.
- If counter‑clockwise, it is S.
Thus we obtain (R)-2‑butanol and (S)-2‑butanol, which are non‑superimposable mirror images.
Step 5: Qualitatively, one enantiomer rotates plane‑polarized light to the right (dextrorotatory, “+”), the other to the left (levorotatory, “–”). The actual sign must be measured experimentally.

practice.q: A compound with formula C₅H₁₀ shows two distinct NMR signals for its methyl groups. Propose a structure that explains this observation and state which type of isomerism is involved.
practice.a:
Step 1: C₅H₁₀ suggests one degree of unsaturation – either a double bond or a ring.
Step 2: Two different methyl signals mean the methyl groups are in nonequivalent environments.
Step 3: Choose a cycloalkane that creates nonequivalent methyls: methylcyclobutane.
Structure: a four‑membered ring (cyclobutane) with a CH₃ attached to one carbon. The ring carbons are not all equivalent, so the methyl attached to the ring carbon is different from any hypothetical methyl on the ring (there is only one methyl).
Step 4: The nonequivalence arises from **structural (constitutional) isomerism** – the compound is a different constitutional isomer from, for example, pentene, which would give only one methyl environment.

practice.q: Explain why 1,2‑dichloro‑1,2‑difluoroethane (Cl₂C=CF₂) exhibits both geometric isomerism and optical activity. Draw all stereoisomers and indicate which are meso, which are enantiomeric pairs.
practice.a:
Step 1: The C=C double bond allows cis/trans (geometric) isomerism because each carbon has two different substituents (Cl and F).
Step 2: Draw the four possible arrangements:
- (E)-Cl‑C(=C)‑F with Cl and F opposite on each carbon → trans.
- (Z)-Cl‑C(=C)‑F with Cl and F on the same side → cis.
Step 3: Each geometric isomer contains a stereogenic carbon (each carbon is attached to Cl, F, H (implicit), and the other carbon). Therefore each geometric form can exist as a pair of enantiomers.
Step 4: List them:
1. (E)-trans‑(R,R)
2. (E)-trans‑(S,S) – these are enantiomers.
3. (Z)-cis‑(R,S)
4. (Z)-cis‑(S,R) – these are also enantiomers.
Step 5: Check for internal symmetry. The (E) pair has a plane of symmetry only if the substituents are identical, which they are not (Cl ≠ F), so no meso form. The (Z) pair also lacks a symmetry plane because the two substituents differ. Hence **all four stereoisomers are chiral**; there is no meso form.
Step 6: Therefore the molecule shows both geometric (E/Z) isomerism and optical activity (four enantiomeric stereoisomers).

practice.q: A compound A (C₈H₁₀O₂) exists as two constitutional isomers: an ester and a carboxylic acid. Isomer B is a geometric isomer of the ester form. Provide the structures of A (both isomers) and B, and explain how IR spectroscopy could be used to distinguish among them.
practice.a:
Step 1: Write the ester constitutional isomer – methyl benzoate:
Ph‑C(=O)‑O‑CH₃ (phenyl ring attached to carbonyl, then O‑CH₃).
Step 2: Write the carboxylic acid constitutional isomer – benzoic acid:
Ph‑C(=O)‑OH.
Both have formula C₈H₁₀O₂.
Step 3: The ester can have a geometric (cis/trans) isomer only if the carbonyl carbon is part of a C=C system; instead we consider the *cis/trans* of the aromatic ring relative to the carbonyl in an *ortho‑substituted* derivative. Choose an ortho‑substituted ester such as o‑methyl cinnamate (Ph‑CH=CH‑C(=O)‑OCH₃). Its *E* (trans) form is the more stable geometric isomer; the *Z* (cis) form is isomer B.
Thus:
- A (ester, trans): **trans‑o‑methyl cinnamate** (Ph‑CH=CH‑C(=O)‑OCH₃, with the phenyl and OCH₃ on opposite sides of the C=C).
- B (cis): **cis‑o‑methyl cinnamate** (same connectivity, phenyl and OCH₃ on the same side).
Step 4: IR distinctions:
- Ester carbonyl shows a strong C=O stretch near 1735 cm⁻¹; carboxylic acid carbonyl appears slightly lower (~1710 cm⁻¹) and is broadened by O‑H hydrogen bonding.
- Carboxylic acid also shows a very broad O‑H stretch around 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, absent in the ester.
- The geometric isomers of the ester give different C=C stretch frequencies: trans‑C=C around 1620 cm⁻¹, cis‑C=C slightly higher (~1650 cm⁻¹).
Therefore, by examining the carbonyl region, the O‑H region, and the C=C stretch, IR spectroscopy can differentiate the carboxylic acid from the ester and also tell the trans from the cis geometric isomer.

recap: Isomerism occurs when compounds share the same molecular formula but differ in how their atoms are arranged. Structural isomers have different connectivity, geometric (cis/trans) isomers have the same connectivity but differ around a double bond or ring, and optical isomers are non‑superimposable mirror images caused by chirality. These differences lead to distinct physical and chemical properties.

key_terms.meaning: Existence of two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.
Isomers that differ in the order in which atoms are bonded.
Isomers with the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement around a restricted bond.
Property of a molecule that makes it non‑superimposable on its mirror image.
One of a pair of chiral molecules that are mirror images of each other.
The ability of a chiral substance to rotate plane‑polarized light.
A carbon atom attached to four different substituents, creating handedness.
A device that allows light waves vibrating in only one plane to pass through.

quiz.q: Which type of isomerism involves a change in the order of atom connectivity?
quiz.why: Structural isomers differ by which atoms are bonded to each other.

quiz.q: In a cis‑trans isomer, what prevents free rotation around the bond?
quiz.why: A double bond or a ring creates a rigid framework that blocks rotation.

quiz.q: A carbon attached to –CH₃, –Cl, –OH, and –H is an example of:
quiz.why: Four different substituents make the carbon a chiral (asymmetric) centre.

quiz.q: Which phenomenon is measured with a polarimeter?
quiz.why: A polarimeter detects the rotation of plane‑polarized light by chiral substances.

quiz.q: C₄H₁₀O can exist as CH₃‑CH₂‑CH₂‑CH₂‑OH and CH₃‑CH(OH)‑CH₃‑CH₃. These two compounds are:
quiz.why: They have the same formula but different connectivity of the –OH group.

quiz.q: Which pair of compounds would be enantiomers?
quiz.why: R‑ and S‑lactic acid are non‑superimposable mirror images.

flashcards.back: Same molecular formula, different arrangement of atoms.
Different connectivity of atoms; bonds are broken/re‑made.
Same connectivity, different spatial arrangement around a double bond or ring.
Molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image; often due to a chiral centre.
One of a pair of chiral molecules that are mirror images of each other.
Rotation of plane‑polarized light by a chiral substance.
Carbon attached to four different groups, giving rise to handedness.
Device that allows only light vibrating in one plane to pass, creating plane‑polarized light.
